Model Test 1.question: ১) Which organelle helps in synthesis of steroids?
Model Test 1.exp:
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) is the principal site of steroid hormone synthesis and lipid metabolism. It is abundant in steroid-producing cells of the adrenal cortex, testes, ovaries, and placenta. The SER is also involved in detoxification of drugs and glycogen metabolism.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Rough ER – synthesizes proteins destined for secretion or membranes.

  • Golgi bodies – modify, package, and sort proteins and lipids.

  • Ribosomes – are the sites of protein synthesis, not steroid synthesis.

Model Test 1.question: ২) Which is not true about mitochondria?
Model Test 1.option3: mitochondrial matrix contain both DNA & RNA
Model Test 1.exp:
Mitochondria are inherited almost exclusively from the mother (maternal inheritance) because the sperm contributes virtually no mitochondria to the fertilized ovum.

The other statements are true:

  • Powerhouse of the cell – Mitochondria generate ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.

  • Krebs (TCA) cycle occurs here – It takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.

  • Mitochondrial matrix contains both DNA and RNA – Mitochondria possess their own circular DNA, RNA, and ribosomes, enabling synthesis of some mitochondrial proteins.

Model Test 1.question: ৩) Barr bodies appear during ---?
Model Test 1.exp:
A Barr body is the condensed, inactive X chromosome (sex chromatin) present in the nuclei of female somatic cells. It is visible during interphase, when the nuclear membrane is intact and chromatin is not condensed into chromosomes.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Mitosis – the nuclear membrane disappears, and Barr bodies are not visible.

  • Meiosis – Barr bodies are not observed.

  • Diakinesis – a stage of prophase I of meiosis; Barr bodies are absent.

Exam pearl:

  • Number of Barr bodies = Number of X chromosomes − 1

    • 46,XX → 1 Barr body

    • 45,X (Turner syndrome) → 0 Barr bodies

    • 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) → 1 Barr body

    • 47,XXX → 2 Barr bodies

Model Test 1.question: ৪) Tetrad formation occurs in which stage of cell division?
৫) Non disjunction occurs in which stage of cell division?
Model Test 1.exp:
Nondisjunction is the failure of homologous chromosomes (Anaphase I) or sister chromatids (Anaphase II or mitosis) to separate properly during anaphase. This results in cells with an abnormal number of chromosomes (aneuploidy), such as:

  • Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)

  • Turner syndrome (45,X)

  • Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Prophase – chromosomes condense and pair (in meiosis).

  • Metaphase – chromosomes align at the equatorial plate.

  • Telophase – daughter nuclei are formed after chromosome separation.

Exam pearl:

  • Anaphase I: Failure of homologous chromosomes to separate → nondisjunction.

  • Anaphase II: Failure of sister chromatids to separate → nondisjunction.

Model Test 1.question: ৬) Which is not a non-sence codon?
Model Test 1.exp:
Nonsense (stop) codons are codons that terminate protein synthesis and do not code for any amino acid. The three stop codons are:

  • UAA – Ochre

  • UAG – Amber

  • UGA – Opal (Umber)

UCA is not a stop codon. It codes for the amino acid Serine.

Model Test 1.question: ৭) Which type of chromosome is not usually present in human body?
Model Test 1.exp:
Human chromosomes are classified according to the position of the centromere:

  • Metacentric  – Centromere is in the middle; arms are of equal length.

  • Submetacentric  – Centromere is slightly off-center; one arm is shorter.

  • Acrocentric – Centromere is near one end; chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22 are acrocentric.

  • Telocentric – Centromere is at the terminal end, producing only one visible arm. Telocentric chromosomes are not normally found in humans, although they occur in some other species (e.g., mice).

Model Test 1.question: ৮) In appositional growth the cartilage increases in----?
Model Test 1.exp:
Appositional growth is the growth of cartilage by the addition of new layers on its surface from the inner (chondrogenic) layer of the perichondrium. This results in an increase in the width (thickness) of the cartilage.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Length increases by interstitial growth, where chondrocytes divide within the cartilage matrix.

  • Height is not the characteristic feature of appositional growth.

  • B + C is incorrect because appositional growth specifically increases width, not height.

Exam pearl:

  • Appositional growth → ↑ Width (perichondrium)

  • Interstitial growth → ↑ Length (division of chondrocytes within cartilage)

Model Test 1.question: ৯) Menisci of knee is example of---?
Model Test 1.exp:
The menisci of the knee are composed of fibrocartilage (white fibrocartilage). Fibrocartilage is rich in type I collagen, making it strong and resistant to compression and tensile forces.

Other examples of fibrocartilage include:

  • Intervertebral discs

  • Pubic symphysis

  • Articular discs (e.g., TMJ)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Cellular cartilage is not a recognized type of cartilage.

  • Hyaline cartilage is found in articular surfaces, trachea, nose, and costal cartilages.

  • Elastic cartilage is found in the pinna, epiglottis, and auditory tube.

Model Test 1.question: ১০) Atavistic epiphysis is present in---?
Model Test 1.exp:
An atavistic epiphysis is an epiphysis that represents a bone that was separate in lower vertebrates but has fused with another bone during evolution.

The coracoid process of the scapula is the classic example of an atavistic epiphysis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Head of femur – a pressure epiphysis.

  • Greater trochanter of femur – a traction epiphysis.

  • Tubercle of humerus – a traction epiphysis.

Exam pearl:

  • Pressure epiphysis → Head of femur, head of humerus.

  • Traction epiphysis → Greater trochanter, tubercles of humerus.

  • Atavistic epiphysis → Coracoid process of scapula.

Model Test 1.question: ১১) Which type of bone cell is present in Howship’s lacunae?
Model Test 1.exp:
Howship's lacunae (resorption bays) are shallow depressions on the surface of bone formed during bone resorption. They contain osteoclasts, which are large, multinucleated cells derived from the monocyte–macrophage lineage and are responsible for breaking down bone matrix.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Osteoprogenitor cells – precursor cells that differentiate into osteoblasts.

  • Osteocytes – mature bone cells located within lacunae inside the bone matrix (not Howship's lacunae).

  • Osteoblasts – bone-forming cells found on the bone surface.

Exam pearl:

  • Howship's lacunae → Osteoclasts (bone resorption)

  • Lacunae → Osteocytes (mature bone cells)

Model Test 1.question: ১২) The mucous membrane of urinary bladder is lined by---?
Model Test 1.exp:
The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a specialized stratified epithelium that allows the bladder to stretch and recoil as it fills and empties with urine.

Key features of transitional epithelium:

  • Multilayered epithelium

  • Surface umbrella (dome-shaped) cells

  • Impermeable to urine

  • Lines the renal pelvis, ureters, urinary bladder, and proximal urethra

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Simple columnar epithelium – lines the stomach and intestines.

  • Pseudostratified epithelium – lines most of the respiratory tract.

  • Simple cuboidal epithelium – lines kidney tubules and thyroid follicles.

Model Test 1.question: ১৩) Mammary gland is an example of ---gland?
Model Test 1.exp:
The mammary gland is classically classified as a modified apocrine gland.

  • Lipid (fat) secretion occurs by the apocrine mechanism, where the apical portion of the cell is pinched off.

  • Protein secretion occurs by the merocrine mechanism (exocytosis).

Because the characteristic mode of milk fat secretion is apocrine, the best single answer is Apocrine.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Holocrine – entire cell disintegrates to release secretion (e.g., sebaceous glands).

  • Merocrine – secretion by exocytosis without loss of cytoplasm (e.g., salivary glands, pancreas, eccrine sweat glands).

  • Epicrine – not a recognized mode of glandular secretion.

Exam pearl:

  • Sebaceous gland → Holocrine

  • Mammary gland → Apocrine (modified; fat by apocrine, protein by merocrine)

  • Salivary & pancreatic glands → Merocrine

Model Test 1.question: ১৪) How many principal type of cell are found in ordinary connective tissue?
Model Test 1.exp:
Ordinary connective tissue (connective tissue proper) contains 7 principal cell types:

  1. Fibroblasts

  2. Macrophages (histiocytes)

  3. Mast cells

  4. Plasma cells

  5. Adipocytes (fat cells)

  6. Undifferentiated mesenchymal (stem) cells

  7. Wandering leukocytes (e.g., lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils)

Model Test 1.question: ১৫) Which is not a criteria of cardiac muscle?
Model Test 1.exp:
Cardiac muscle fibers are branched, not unbranched. Their characteristic features include:

  • Cross striations 

  • One (occasionally two) centrally placed nucleus 

  • Branching muscle fibers 

  • Intercalated discs connecting adjacent cardiac muscle cells 

The other options are true features of cardiac muscle:

  • Cross striation – present.

  • Centrally placed nuclei – characteristic.

  • Intercalated discs – unique junctions providing mechanical and electrical coupling.

Model Test 1.question: ১৬) Which organelle produces lysosome?
Model Test 1.exp:
Lysosomes are formed by the Golgi apparatus, which packages hydrolytic enzymes synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum into membrane-bound vesicles to form primary lysosomes.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Endoplasmic reticulum – synthesizes proteins (RER) and lipids (SER); lysosomal enzymes are synthesized in the RER but lysosomes are formed by the Golgi apparatus.

  • Centrioles – organize the mitotic spindle during cell division.

  • Ribosomes – sites of protein synthesis.

Exam pearl:

  • RER → Synthesizes lysosomal enzymes.

  • Golgi apparatus → Modifies, packages, and forms lysosomes.

Model Test 1.question: ১৭) Which event initiates cardiac cycle?
Model Test 1.exp:
The cardiac cycle begins with atrial systole, which is triggered by depolarization of the atria (P wave on ECG). During atrial systole:

  • The atria contract.

  • The final 20–30% of ventricular filling ("atrial kick") occurs.

  • This is followed by ventricular systole.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Atrial diastole occurs after atrial contraction.

  • Ventricular systole follows atrial systole.

  • Ventricular diastole occurs after ventricular systole.

Exam pearl:
Sequence of the cardiac cycle:

  1. Atrial systole

  2. Isovolumetric ventricular contraction

  3. Ventricular ejection

  4. Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation

  5. Ventricular filling

Model Test 1.question: ১৮) Ventricular repolarization is represented by---in ECG?
Model Test 1.exp:
The T wave on the ECG represents ventricular repolarization, the process by which the ventricles recover electrically after contraction.

ECG wave summary:

  • P wave → Atrial depolarization

  • QRS complex → Ventricular depolarization

  • T wave → Ventricular repolarization 

  • ST segment → Period when the ventricles are completely depolarized (plateau phase of the ventricular action potential)

Exam pearl:

  • P = Atrial depolarization

  • QRS = Ventricular depolarization

  • T = Ventricular repolarization

Model Test 1.question: ১৯) Cardiac output decreases in---?
Model Test 1.exp:
Cardiac output (CO = Heart Rate × Stroke Volume) is decreased in heart disease, particularly in conditions such as heart failure, cardiomyopathy, and severe valvular heart disease, where the heart's pumping ability is impaired.

The other options are incorrect because they are associated with increased cardiac output:

  • Anemia – Increased CO to compensate for reduced oxygen-carrying capacity.

  • Thyrotoxicosis – Increased metabolic demand and heart rate increase CO.

  • Pregnancy – CO increases by approximately 30–50% due to increased blood volume and metabolic demands.

Model Test 1.question: ২০) What is the intermediate acting blood pressure regulating mechanism?
Model Test 1.exp:
Blood pressure is regulated by three major mechanisms based on the time of action:

  • Short-term (seconds to minutes):

    • Baroreceptor mechanism

    • Chemoreceptor mechanism

  • Intermediate-term (minutes to hours):

    • Capillary fluid shift mechanism

    • Stress relaxation of blood vessels

    • Renin–angiotensin system (early phase)

  • Long-term (hours to days):

    • Renal body fluid mechanism (pressure diuresis and natriuresis)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Baroreceptor mechanism – Short-term regulation.

  • Chemoreceptor mechanism – Short-term regulation.

  • Renal body fluid mechanism – Long-term regulation.

Model Test 1.question: ২১) Which type of shock occurs in cardiac tamponade?
Model Test 1.exp:
Cardiac tamponade causes obstructive shock because fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac compresses the heart, preventing adequate ventricular filling during diastole. This leads to:

  • Reduced venous return

  • Decreased stroke volume

  • Decreased cardiac output

  • Hypotension

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hypovolemic shock – Due to loss of blood or body fluids.

  • Neurogenic shock – Due to loss of sympathetic vascular tone (e.g., spinal cord injury).

  • Cardiogenic shock – Due to primary pump failure (e.g., acute myocardial infarction, severe cardiomyopathy).

Exam pearl:
Common causes of obstructive shock:

  • Cardiac tamponade

  • Tension pneumothorax

  • Massive pulmonary embolism

Model Test 1.question: ২২) What is the amount of blood Flow to adrenal gland under basal conditions?
Model Test 1.exp:
The adrenal gland has one of the highest blood flows per unit weight of any organ. Under basal conditions, adrenal blood flow is approximately:

300 mL/min/100 g of tissue

This rich blood supply is essential for the rapid secretion of adrenal hormones into the circulation.

The other options are incorrect because they are lower or higher than the normal basal adrenal blood flow.

Model Test 1.question: ২৩) What is not a characteristics of oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve?
Model Test 1.exp:
The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve describes the relationship between the partial pressure of oxygen (PO₂) and hemoglobin saturation. Oxygen binding to hemoglobin is reversible, allowing oxygen to be loaded in the lungs and unloaded in the tissues.

The other options are correct because:

  • Sigmoid shape – Due to cooperative binding of oxygen to hemoglobin.

  • Begins from 0 level – At PO₂ of 0 mmHg, hemoglobin saturation is essentially 0%.

  • Consists of two zones – A steep portion (facilitates oxygen unloading in tissues) and a plateau portion (facilitates oxygen loading in the lungs).

Model Test 1.question: ২৪) PCO2 in alveoli is--?
Model Test 1.exp:
The normal partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO₂) in the alveoli is approximately 40 mmHg, which is nearly equal to the arterial PCO₂ under normal physiological conditions.

Normal alveolar gas values:

  • PO₂: ~104 mmHg

  • PCO₂: 40 mmHg

  • Water vapor pressure (PH₂O): 47 mmHg

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 45–47 mmHg are higher than the normal alveolar PCO₂ and are more consistent with hypoventilation or venous blood values.

Model Test 1.question: ২৫) Functional residual capacity is equal to--?
Model Test 1.exp:
Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal (tidal) expiration.

Formula:
FRC = Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) + Residual Volume (RV)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • TV + IRV = Inspiratory Capacity (IC)

  • IRV + TV = Inspiratory Capacity (IC)

  • VC + RV = Total Lung Capacity (TLC)

Lung volume formulas (High-yield):

  • IC = TV + IRV

  • FRC = ERV + RV

  • VC = IRV + TV + ERV

  • TLC = VC + RV

Model Test 1.question: ২৬) Which one isn't chemotactic agent for neutrophil?
Model Test 1.exp:
MCP-1 (Monocyte Chemoattractant Protein-1, CCL2) is a chemokine that primarily attracts monocytes, not neutrophils.

The other options are important chemotactic agents for neutrophils:

  • C5a – Potent complement-derived neutrophil chemoattractant.

  • LTB₄ (Leukotriene B₄) – Strong chemoattractant and activator of neutrophils.

  • IL-8 (CXCL8) – Major chemokine responsible for neutrophil chemotaxis and activation.

High-yield neutrophil chemotactic factors:

  • C5a

  • IL-8 (CXCL8)

  • LTB₄

  • Bacterial products (e.g., N-formyl peptides)

Model Test 1.question: ২৭) All of the following are physiological giant cell except...?
Model Test 1.exp:
Langhans giant cells are pathological giant cells formed by the fusion of activated macrophages. They are characteristically seen in granulomatous inflammation, such as tuberculosis, where the nuclei are arranged peripherally in a horseshoe pattern.

The other options are physiological giant cells:

  • Osteoclast – Multinucleated bone-resorbing cell.

  • Megakaryocyte – Large multinucleated bone marrow cell that produces platelets.

  • Syncytiotrophoblast – Multinucleated layer of the placenta involved in hormone secretion and maternal-fetal exchange.

Model Test 1.question: ২৮) Which one is not true about chronic inflammation?
Model Test 1.exp:
Chronic inflammation is characterized by:

  • Duration of weeks to months (or longer).

  • Vascular phenomena are less prominent than in acute inflammation.

  • Simultaneous tissue destruction and repair (fibrosis and angiogenesis).

  • Predominantly mononuclear cell infiltration (macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells).

The other options are correct because:

  • Usual duration weeks to months – Characteristic of chronic inflammation.

  • Vascular phenomenon not prominent – True; vascular changes are more marked in acute inflammation.

  • Repair process starts concurrently – True; healing occurs alongside ongoing inflammation.

Exudation is a hallmark of acute inflammation, not chronic inflammation.

Model Test 1.question: ২৯) Skin blister produced by burn is an example of....... inflammation?
Model Test 1.exp:
A skin blister produced by a burn is a classic example of serous inflammation. It results from the accumulation of clear, protein-poor serous fluid beneath the epidermis, forming a blister.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fibrinous inflammation – Characterized by fibrin deposition on serosal surfaces (e.g., fibrinous pericarditis, pleuritis).

  • Pseudomembranous inflammation – Characterized by a pseudomembrane, as seen in diphtheria and Clostridioides difficile colitis.

  • Suppurative inflammation – Characterized by pus formation due to neutrophilic infiltration (e.g., abscess).

Model Test 1.question: ৩০) Which of the following is the correct sequence of steps involved in phagocytosis?
Model Test 1.exp:
Phagocytosis occurs through a series of steps. The process begins with chemotaxis of phagocytes toward the site of infection, followed by adhesion and recognition of the particle, engulfment forming a phagosome, and finally killing and digestion after fusion with lysosomes.

High-yield points:

  • Main steps of phagocytosis → Chemotaxis → Adhesion → Engulfment → Killing and digestion

  • Neutrophils and macrophages are the major phagocytic cells.

  • Opsonization by IgG and C3b enhances phagocytosis.

Model Test 1.question: ৩১) Hypoxic death of cells within brain is a type of........ necrosis.
Model Test 1.exp:
Hypoxic (ischemic) death of cells in the brain results in liquefactive necrosis. This occurs because the brain contains abundant hydrolytic enzymes and relatively little supporting connective tissue, leading to enzymatic digestion of dead tissue into a liquid mass.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Coagulative necrosis – Typical of ischemic infarction in solid organs such as the heart, kidney, and spleen (except the brain).

  • Caseous necrosis – Characteristic of tuberculosis and some fungal infections.

  • Fibrinoid necrosis – Seen in immune-mediated vasculitis and severe hypertension affecting blood vessel walls.

Exam pearl:

  • Brain infarction → Liquefactive necrosis

  • All other solid organ infarctions → Coagulative necrosis

Model Test 1.question: ৩২) Dry gangrene occurs due to lack of........ to tissues.
Model Test 1.exp:
Dry gangrene results from loss of arterial blood supply (ischemia) to a tissue, most commonly affecting the lower limbs in patients with atherosclerosis or diabetes mellitus. The affected tissue becomes dry, shriveled, black, and mummified due to coagulative necrosis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Venous drainage obstruction is more commonly associated with congestion and may contribute to wet gangrene, not dry gangrene.

  • Nerve supply loss does not directly cause gangrene.

  • Both arterial supply and venous drainage is not the primary mechanism of dry gangrene.

Exam pearl:

  • Dry gangrene → Arterial occlusion, coagulative necrosis, no infection.

  • Wet gangrene → Ischemia with superimposed infection, liquefactive changes.

  • Gas gangrene → Clostridium perfringens infection.

Model Test 1.question: ৩৩) What type of metaplasia occurs in Barrett's oesophagus?
Model Test 1.exp:
Barrett's oesophagus is characterized by columnar (intestinal) metaplasia, in which the normal non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the distal oesophagus is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells due to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Squamous metaplasia – Replacement of columnar epithelium by squamous epithelium (e.g., in smokers' bronchi).

  • Connective tissue metaplasia – Formation of bone or cartilage in connective tissue.

  • Tumour metaplasia – Not a recognized type of metaplasia.

Exam pearl:

  • GERD → Barrett's oesophagus → Intestinal (columnar) metaplasia → Increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

Model Test 1.question: ৩৪) Cumulative sublethal injury over long life span results in which of the following?
Model Test 1.exp:
Cellular aging results from the cumulative effects of repeated sublethal injury over a long lifespan. Progressive damage from oxidative stress, DNA damage, telomere shortening, and reduced repair capacity leads to a gradual decline in cellular function.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Cellular swelling – An early, reversible manifestation of acute cell injury.

  • Intracellular accumulation – Refers to the buildup of lipids, proteins, pigments, or other substances within cells, not the overall consequence of lifelong sublethal injury.

  • Pathological calcification – Deposition of calcium in damaged or normal tissues, unrelated to cumulative aging.

Model Test 1.question: ৩৫) Fragmentation of pyknotic nucleus is called....?
Model Test 1.exp:
Karyorrhexis is the fragmentation of a pyknotic nucleus during irreversible cell injury and necrosis.

Nuclear changes in necrosis occur in sequence:

  1. Pyknosis – Nuclear shrinkage with increased basophilia.

  2. Karyorrhexis – Fragmentation of the pyknotic nucleus.

  3. Karyolysis – Dissolution of the nucleus due to enzymatic degradation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pyknosis – Nuclear shrinkage, not fragmentation.

  • Karyolysis – Complete dissolution/fading of the nucleus.

  • Karyokinesis – Normal division of the nucleus during mitosis.

Exam pearl:

  • Pyknosis → Karyorrhexis → Karyolysis

Model Test 1.question: ৩৬) CA-125 is a specific tumor marker for....?
Model Test 1.exp:
CA-125 (Cancer Antigen 125) is the most widely used tumor marker for epithelial ovarian carcinoma. It is primarily used to:

  • Monitor response to treatment.

  • Detect recurrence.

  • Support the diagnosis in women with an adnexal mass (it is not suitable as a screening test).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Testicular tumor – AFP and β-hCG are the principal tumor markers.

  • Prostate cancer – PSA (Prostate-Specific Antigen) is the characteristic marker.

  • Liver cell cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma) – AFP (Alpha-fetoprotein) is the classic marker.

High-yield tumor markers:

  • CA-125 → Ovarian carcinoma

  • PSA → Prostate carcinoma

  • AFP → Hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk sac tumor

  • CEA → Colorectal carcinoma (monitoring)

  • CA 19-9 → Pancreatic carcinoma

Model Test 1.question: ৩৭) Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is associated with which oncogenic virus?
Model Test 1.exp:
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is strongly associated with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), particularly the undifferentiated (non-keratinizing) type. EBV infects epithelial cells and B lymphocytes and plays an important role in tumor development.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Human papillomavirus (HPV) – Associated with cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal cancers.

  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) – Not an established oncogenic virus.

  • Hepatitis B virus (HBV) – Associated with hepatocellular carcinoma.

High-yield oncogenic viruses:

  • EBV → Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma

  • HPV (16, 18) → Cervical, anal, oropharyngeal cancers

  • HBV, HCV → Hepatocellular carcinoma

  • HTLV-1 → Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma

Model Test 1.question: ৩৮) Which one is a malignant tumor?
Model Test 1.exp:
Lymphoma is a malignant neoplasm arising from lymphoid tissue (B cells, T cells, or NK cells). It includes Hodgkin lymphoma and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

The other options are benign tumors:

  • Meningioma – Usually a benign tumor of the meninges.

  • Chondroma – Benign tumor of cartilage.

  • Lymphangioma – Benign lymphatic malformation (hamartomatous lesion).

High-yield examples:

  • Benign: Adenoma, Lipoma, Chondroma, Meningioma

  • Malignant: Carcinoma, Sarcoma, Lymphoma, Melanoma

Model Test 1.question: ৩৯) Hypersegmented neutrophil is a characteristic feature of....?
Model Test 1.exp:
Hypersegmented neutrophils (neutrophils with ≥6 nuclear lobes) are a characteristic peripheral blood smear finding in megaloblastic anemia, which results from vitamin B₁₂ or folate deficiency due to defective DNA synthesis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ALL – Characterized by lymphoblasts, not hypersegmented neutrophils.

  • AML – Characterized by myeloblasts and Auer rods.

  • Sickle cell anemia – Characterized by sickled red cells, target cells, and Howell–Jolly bodies (especially after splenectomy), not hypersegmented neutrophils.

High-yield pearl:

  • Hypersegmented neutrophils + macro-ovalocytes → Megaloblastic anemia (Vitamin B₁₂/Folate deficiency).

Model Test 1.question: ৪০) Which is not true about intravascular hemolysis?
Model Test 1.exp:
Intravascular hemolysis occurs when red blood cells are destroyed within the circulation, releasing free hemoglobin into the plasma.

Its characteristic features include:

  • Hemoglobinemia – Free hemoglobin in plasma.

  • Hemoglobinuria – Hemoglobin excreted in urine.

  • Hemosiderinuria – Iron-containing hemosiderin appears in urine after renal tubular cells slough off.

The other options are correct features of intravascular hemolysis. Splenomegaly is more characteristic of extravascular hemolysis, where red blood cells are destroyed by macrophages in the spleen.

High-yield comparison:

  • Intravascular hemolysis: Hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria, ↓ haptoglobin.

  • Extravascular hemolysis: Splenomegaly, jaundice, pigment gallstones.

Model Test 1.question: ৪১) Which nerve is derived from 3rd pharyngeal arch?
Model Test 1.exp:
Each pharyngeal arch is associated with a specific cranial nerve:

  • 1st pharyngeal arch → Mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3)

  • 2nd pharyngeal arch → Facial nerve (CN VII)

  • 3rd pharyngeal arch → Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

  • 4th & 6th pharyngeal arches → Vagus nerve (CN X)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Mandibular nerve (V3) – 1st arch.

  • Facial nerve (VII) – 2nd arch.

  • Vagus nerve (X) – 4th and 6th arches.

High-yield mnemonic:

  • 1 → V

  • 2 → VII

  • 3 → IX

  • 4 & 6 → X

Model Test 1.question: ৪২) which one is not a derivative of ureteric bud?
Model Test 1.exp:
The ureteric bud gives rise to the collecting system of the kidney, including:

  • Ureter

  • Renal pelvis

  • Major and minor calyces

  • Collecting ducts/tubules

The urethra is derived from the urogenital sinus, not the ureteric bud.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ureter – Derived from ureteric bud.

  • Renal pelvis – Derived from ureteric bud.

  • Collecting tubules – Derived from ureteric bud.

High-yield embryology:

  • Ureteric bud → Collecting system

  • Metanephric blastema → Nephrons (glomerulus, PCT, loop of Henle, DCT)

Model Test 1.question: ৪৩) Which gland is ectodermal in origin?
Model Test 1.exp:
The parotid gland is ectodermal in origin, developing from the oral ectoderm.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Submandibular gland – Derived from endoderm of the floor of the mouth.

  • Thymus – Derived from endoderm of the third pharyngeal pouch.

  • Thyroid gland – Derived from endoderm of the floor of the primitive pharynx.

High-yield embryology:

  • Parotid gland → Ectoderm

  • Submandibular & sublingual glands → Endoderm

  • Thyroid → Endoderm

Model Test 1.question: ৪৪) Derivatives of foregut excludes.....?
Model Test 1.exp:
The foregut gives rise to:

  • Whole oesophagus

  • Whole stomach

  • Proximal part of duodenum (up to the opening of the bile duct)

  • Liver, gallbladder, biliary system

  • Pancreas

The duodenum is not entirely a foregut derivative. Its distal part is derived from the midgut.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Whole oesophagus – Foregut derivative.

  • Whole stomach – Foregut derivative.

  • Whole pancreas – Foregut derivative (from dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds).

High-yield embryology:

  • Foregut: Oesophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, pancreas

  • Midgut: Distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal 2/3 transverse colon

  • Hindgut: Distal 1/3 transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, upper anal canal

Model Test 1.question: ৪৫) Cyanosis doesn't occur in all of the following except...?
Model Test 1.exp:
Cyanosis occurs when there is an increased amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin (>5 g/dL) in blood.

Pulmonary oedema can cause cyanosis due to impaired oxygen exchange and resulting hypoxemia.

The other options generally do not produce cyanosis:

  • Anemia – Total hemoglobin is reduced, so deoxygenated hemoglobin may not reach the level required for cyanosis.

  • CO poisoning – Produces carboxyhemoglobinemia; blood may appear cherry red, not cyanotic.

  • Histotoxic hypoxia – Oxygen cannot be utilized by tissues (e.g., cyanide poisoning), but arterial oxygenation is usually normal.

Model Test 1.question: ৪৬) CO poisoning is a form of....... hypoxia?
Model Test 1.exp:
Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning causes anemic hypoxia because CO binds strongly with hemoglobin (about 200–250 times more affinity than oxygen) forming carboxyhemoglobin, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Stagnant (circulatory) hypoxia – Due to reduced blood flow to tissues (e.g., heart failure, shock).

  • Ischemic hypoxia – A type of stagnant hypoxia due to localized reduction in blood supply.

  • Histotoxic hypoxia – Occurs when tissues cannot utilize oxygen (e.g., cyanide poisoning).

High-yield hypoxia classification:

  • Hypoxic hypoxia → Low arterial PO₂ (e.g., pneumonia, high altitude)

  • Anemic hypoxia → Reduced O₂ carrying capacity (e.g., anemia, CO poisoning)

  • Stagnant hypoxia → Reduced blood flow (e.g., shock, heart failure)

  • Histotoxic hypoxia → Failure of cellular oxygen utilization (e.g., cyanide)

Model Test 1.question: ৪৭) Central chemoreceptor cells primarily respond to changes in which of the following?
Model Test 1.exp:
Central chemoreceptor cells located in the medulla oblongata primarily respond to changes in CO₂ concentration in arterial blood. CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier and reacts with water in cerebrospinal fluid to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. The increased H⁺ concentration in CSF stimulates central chemoreceptors and increases ventilation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • O₂ concentration in arterial blood – Mainly detected by peripheral chemoreceptors located in the carotid and aortic bodies, especially when PaO₂ falls significantly.

  • HCO₃⁻ concentration in cerebrospinal fluid – HCO₃⁻ helps buffer changes in CSF pH but is not the primary stimulus for central chemoreceptor activation.

  • Blood pH directly – Central chemoreceptors do not directly sense blood pH because H⁺ cannot cross the blood–brain barrier effectively; they respond to CSF H⁺ generated from CO₂.

High-yield points:

  • Central chemoreceptors → CO₂ (via CSF H⁺)

  • Peripheral chemoreceptors → O₂, CO₂, and blood pH

  • Main regulator of normal ventilation → CO₂ level

Model Test 1.question: ৪৮) which factor doesn't play any role in preventing collapse of the lungs?
Model Test 1.exp:
The correct answer is elastic recoil force. The elastic recoil property of the lungs tends to collapse the lungs inward rather than prevent collapse. It is an inward-directed force produced by elastic fibres of lung tissue and surface tension, opposing lung expansion.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Surfactants – Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse, especially at the end of expiration.

  • Residual volume – The presence of residual volume keeps some air within the lungs after maximal expiration and helps prevent complete lung collapse.

  • Intrapleural pressure – Negative intrapleural pressure maintains lung expansion by keeping the lungs attached to the chest wall.

High-yield points:

  • Factors preventing lung collapse → surfactant, residual volume, negative intrapleural pressure

  • Elastic recoil force → promotes lung collapse and is responsible for passive expiration

Model Test 1.question: ৪৯) Which one is not a vitamin K dependent clotting factor?
Model Test 1.exp:
The correct answer is labile factor (Factor V). It is not a vitamin K dependent clotting factor. Vitamin K is required for the synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X in the liver.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Prothrombin (Factor II) – It is a vitamin K dependent clotting factor.

  • Stable factor (Factor X) – It is a vitamin K dependent clotting factor.

  • Christmas factor (Factor IX) – It is a vitamin K dependent clotting factor and deficiency causes haemophilia B.

High-yield points:

  • Vitamin K dependent factors → II, VII, IX, X

  • Mnemonic → "1972" (Factors X, IX, VII, II)

  • Factors not dependent on vitamin K → I, V, VIII, XI, XII, XIII

Model Test 1.question: ৫০) What is the mechanism of blood clotting that occurs in a test tube?
Model Test 1.option4: blood never clots in test tube
Model Test 1.exp:
The correct answer is intrinsic pathway. Blood clotting that occurs in a test tube is initiated when blood comes in contact with a foreign surface such as glass, which activates Factor XII (Hageman factor) and starts the intrinsic coagulation pathway.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Extrinsic pathway – It is initiated by tissue factor (Factor III) released from damaged tissues and mainly operates during tissue injury in the body.

  • Both intrinsic & extrinsic pathway – Although both pathways converge at the common pathway (Factor X activation), clotting in a plain test tube is classically due to activation of the intrinsic pathway.

  • Blood never clots in test tube – Incorrect because blood readily clots in a test tube if anticoagulants are not added.

High-yield points:

  • Test tube clotting → Intrinsic pathway

  • Tissue injury → Extrinsic pathway

  • Common pathway → Factor X → thrombin → fibrin formation
